title: Inside the Mind of a Master Teacher: Here's How Lynsay Fabio Would Approach Classroom Management During Distance Learning oach-classroom-management-during-distance-learning
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
source: Dave Stuart Jr. (davestuartjr.com), guest post by Lynsay Mills Fabio, September 3, 2020
summary: In this guest post on Dave Stuart Jr.'s blog, veteran classroom-management educator Lynsay Mills Fabio thinks aloud through exactly how she would build a classroom management plan for distance learning, having reached out to roughly 700 teachers who named virtual classroom management as their top fall concern. She insists the work must start internally — sitting quietly to rehearse the truth that 'I am the right person for this job' before making any structural decisions — and then proceeds through a detailed 'walkthrough' method, mentally rehearsing a lesson minute by minute from a student's perspective before writing rules or procedures. Fabio adapts her tried-and-true in-person rules (drawn from Michael Linsin's framework) rule by rule for a Zoom environment, working through thorny questions like whether cameras should be mandatory, how to handle side conversations, and how students should signal leaving their seats, landing on a five-rule, three-consequence plan. Throughout, she argues for erring toward more control at the start of the year since loosening restrictions later is far easier than tightening them, and she closes by distinguishing classroom management (the 'plates') from actual instruction (the 'meal'), warning that even a perfectly managed classroom fails if it isn't in service of real learning.
points: Building a distance-learning management plan should start with an internal step — deliberately rehearsing the belief 'I am the right person for this job' — before any rules or procedures get written, since anxious decision-making produces worse plans.
A detailed 'walkthrough,' mentally rehearsing a lesson minute-by-minute from the student's point of view, is treated as a prerequisite for writing an effective plan, not an optional nicety.
Fabio deliberately errs toward more control at the start of the year because loosening restrictions later is far easier than clawing back freedoms once they've been granted.
Distinguishing classroom management (the 'plates') from actual instruction (the 'meal,' per Doug Lemov) guards against mistaking a well-run virtual classroom for the learning it's supposed to enable.
quotes: Classroom management is about protecting every child's right to learn and enjoy amazing academic experiences.
I am the right person for this job. There is no one with a cape flying in after me. I'm the best we've got right now. I am not perfect, but I am enough.
It's way easier to allow more freedom once I've got the tone I want than to suddenly start taking away freedoms that once existed.
Students are not oblivious — they can tell when their teacher is trying to protect the learning environment rather than just exercising mindless control.

My most basic responsibility as a teacher is to check for their understanding of the lesson as it's happening, and without video, I can't do this — all "hold up your answers" and all hand gestures can't happen without video.
Never mistake good classroom management for the meal itself. But without it, your delicious lesson is going to go to waste.
